newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain Shipments continue high.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain Shipments continue high.

text.p: Heavy wheat shipments dominated quieter but wetter times in Australian grains last week.
Australian Wheat Board (AWB) 1996/97 shipments to February 14, on preliminary figures, amount to a record 6.6 million tonnes, up from 4.6 million tonnes at the same time last year.

"We're really pushing the system," AWB spokesman Alex Nichol said. "We're working to squeeze more out of the logistical system, exploring every possible way (in shipping the record 23 million tonne crop)."
Shipping from New South Wales (NSW) kept "plugging on" with some hiccups, especially in transportation to port, after two consecutive record months, Guy Allen of NSW co-operative GrainCorp said.
Additional equipment for arrival in coming weeks should assist, he said.

The AWB surprised Australian but not international traders by saying on Friday that its record shipping programme may stop it from offering wheat in the latest Pakistan tender for 450,000 tonnes of Australian and U.S. wheat for delivery by April.
The main domestic news during the week was tropical cyclone Gillian, which brought heavy rain to Queensland and northern NSW coastal areas but dissipated at week's end.
Ongoing rain and flash floods, however, had begun to affect sorghum and cotton crops, with implications for new crop wheat.
The week's rain had held up the sorghum harvest in some parts of Queensland, AWB's Nichol said.
The AWB believed rain was unlikely to cause problems in southern Queensland but it could spark some late sorghum sowing in central Queensland, increasing the crop a little.
More rain could cause some move out of sorghum into the sowing of very early wheat, Nichol said.
The week's rain was very beneficial to new crop wheat but had created some damage to sorghum, GrainCorp's Allen said.

Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders also said heavy rain would have an impact on the sorghum crop. Sorghum's price now may hold at current levels, whereas it had earlier seemed likely to ease as the harvest got underway, he said.
A premium on February sorghum disappeared in the past week, showing that needs had been met, while some crop coming off in northern NSW had produced a flat market, he said.
David Lindsay, manager grower services of Namoi Cotton Co-operative, also told Reuters on Friday that heavy rain had waterlogged some cotton crops and threatened to delay picking.
This could reduce the crop from current forecasts of 2.5 million 500-pound bales to about 2.4 million bales, he said.
GrainCorp's Allen described cash grains last week as very frustrating, with a standoff between buyers and sellers.
Cash wheat was steady to choppy in thin trade, ending the week at A$168 Newcastle. Cash sorghum fell by about A$5 a tonne to A$155-A$156 on Friday after reaching A$158.

After a flat week in wheat futures trading, Mitchell sees a correction looming in the mis-matched price structures between Sydney and Chicago, with U.S. prices now seemingly set to rise. Either Australian prices had to fall or Chicago's to rise, he said.
Sydney Futures Exchange prices over the past week were steady in a firm market, with only 19 lots traded and settlement prices mixed in a narrow range.
Mitchell tipped an unchanged AWB pool price on Monday.
